title: 10 Database Concepts You Can't Skip in System Design Interviews
summary: Ten database concepts that come up in system design interviews: indexing, transactions, ACID, isolation levels, MVCC, locking, connection pooling, partitioning, replication and sharding. Each one covers what it is, how it works with a concrete example, its trade-offs and the interview takeaway.

chapters.title: 10 Database Concepts You Can't Skip
points: Cover promise: 10 database concepts that decide how fast, safe and scalable your system is
Single-node foundations: Indexing, Transactions, ACID, Isolation Levels, MVCC, Locking, Connection Pooling
Scaling out: Partitioning, Replication, Sharding
Every concept follows one order: what it is, why it exists, used for, how it works, benefits, things to consider, interview takeaway

chapters.title: Indexing
points: What it is: a separate sorted structure (usually a B-tree) that maps column values to row locations so the DB avoids scanning the whole table
Why it exists: without one, WHERE email = 'a@x.com' on 10M rows is a full scan, O(n); a B-tree lookup is O(log n), about 3-4 page reads
Used for: WHERE filters, JOIN keys, ORDER BY, uniqueness constraints and primary keys

How it works: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_date ON orders(user_id, created_at); the query WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10 walks the tree once and reads 10 entries already sorted, with no sort step
Benefits: reads drop from seconds to milliseconds; sorted output comes for free; a covering index answers the query without touching the table

Things to consider: every index slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and uses disk; composite index column order matters (leftmost prefix rule); low-cardinality columns like boolean gain little; functions on the column (LOWER(email)) bypass the index
Interview takeaway: index the columns you filter, join and sort on, put the most selective equality column first, and say that you pay for faster reads with slower writes

chapters.title: Transactions
points: What it is: a group of reads and writes that the database treats as one unit of work, either fully applied (COMMIT) or fully undone (ROLLBACK)
Why it exists: a crash or error between two related writes would leave data half-updated, for example money debited but never credited
Used for: payments and transfers, order placement plus inventory decrement, and any multi-row or multi-table invariant

How it works: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 100 WHERE id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 100 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT; if the second UPDATE fails, ROLLBACK restores account 1 to its old balance
Benefits: all-or-nothing changes; a consistent view of the data while you work; the write-ahead log (WAL) makes committed work survive a crash

Things to consider: long transactions hold locks and bloat the log, so keep them short and never wait on user input inside one; transactions spanning several services need sagas or 2PC, not a single BEGIN; retry on deadlock or serialization errors
Interview takeaway: wrap every multi-step invariant in one short transaction, and know that it does not stretch across microservices

chapters.title: ACID
points: What it is: four guarantees a transaction gives: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Why it exists: it gives developers a simple mental model: a transaction either happened completely or not at all, whatever crashes or concurrent users do
Used for: choosing a datastore: banking, orders and inventory need ACID; a feed counter or a cache may not

How it works: Atomicity via undo log (rollback); Consistency via constraints (CHECK bal >= 0, FK, UNIQUE); Isolation via locks or MVCC; Durability via WAL flushed to disk (fsync) before COMMIT returns
Benefits: correctness under failure; invariants enforced by the DB rather than app code; predictable behavior under concurrency

Things to consider: ACID costs latency and throughput (fsync per commit, locks); the C in ACID is not the C in CAP; many NoSQL stores trade it for availability and scale (BASE); isolation is a dial, not a switch
Interview takeaway: name each letter with a mechanism (undo log, constraints, MVCC/locks, WAL) and say when you would relax ACID

chapters.title: Isolation Levels
points: What it is: a setting that controls how much one transaction can see of other concurrent transactions' uncommitted or newly committed changes
Why it exists: full isolation (serializable) is slow, so databases offer weaker levels that trade correctness anomalies for throughput
Used for: tuning per workload: Read Committed for most OLTP, Repeatable Read for consistent reports, Serializable for money-critical invariants
How it works: two sessions on balance = 100. T1 reads 100; T2 commits balance = 50; T1 re-reads. Read Committed returns 50 (non-repeatable read); Repeatable Read still returns 100
Benefits: a dial between speed and safety; Read Committed blocks dirty reads, Repeatable Read blocks non-repeatable reads, Serializable blocks every anomaly including write skew

Things to consider: Postgres defaults to Read Committed and MySQL InnoDB to Repeatable Read; stricter levels cause more aborts, so retry on serialization failure (SQLSTATE 40001); write skew (two on-call doctors both leaving) slips past Repeatable Read
Interview takeaway: name the three anomalies (dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom), map each level to what it prevents, and pick the weakest level that keeps your invariant safe

chapters.title: MVCC
points: What it is: Multi-Version Concurrency Control, where the DB keeps several versions of a row and each transaction reads from a snapshot
Why it exists: so readers never block writers and writers never block readers, which lock-only designs cannot do
Used for: Postgres, MySQL InnoDB and Oracle snapshot reads, and implementing Read Committed and Repeatable Read

How it works: in Postgres every row has xmin (creating txn) and xmax (deleting txn). UPDATE users SET plan='pro' WHERE id=7 (txn 120) writes a new row version with xmin=120 and marks the old one xmax=120. A reader whose snapshot predates txn 120 still sees plan='free'
Benefits: high read concurrency with no read locks; consistent point-in-time snapshots; long reports do not stall writers

Things to consider: old versions pile up as dead tuples and need VACUUM (Postgres) or purge (InnoDB); long-running transactions pin old versions and cause bloat; write-write conflicts on the same row still need locks
Interview takeaway: say that MVCC trades extra storage and cleanup for non-blocking reads, and that it is why long transactions hurt even when they only read

chapters.title: Locking
points: What it is: a mechanism where a transaction claims a row, page or table so conflicting writers must wait; shared (S) locks for reads, exclusive (X) locks for writes
Why it exists: MVCC cannot resolve two transactions writing the same row, so something has to serialize them
Used for: preventing lost updates, inventory and seat booking, and queue-style job claiming with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED

How it works: txn A runs SELECT stock FROM items WHERE id=5 FOR UPDATE; txn B running the same statement blocks until A commits, so stock 1 cannot be sold twice. Optimistic alternative: UPDATE items SET stock=stock-1, version=version+1 WHERE id=5 AND version=3, and retry if 0 rows changed
Benefits: pessimistic locks stay safe under high contention; optimistic version checks are cheap and lock-free under low contention; both prevent lost updates

Things to consider: deadlocks when two transactions lock rows in opposite order, so lock in a consistent order; the DB aborts one victim and you must retry; hold locks briefly; table-level locks and escalation kill concurrency
Interview takeaway: use pessimistic locks for hot contended rows, optimistic versions for rare conflicts, and always mention deadlock avoidance and retry

chapters.title: Connection Pooling
points: What it is: a cache of open database connections that the application borrows and returns instead of opening one per request
Why it exists: a new connection costs a TCP and TLS handshake plus authentication, and in Postgres a whole backend process of several MB; thousands of them exhaust memory
Used for: every web service talking to a DB, and for tools like PgBouncer, RDS Proxy and HikariCP that sit between many app instances and the database

How it works: pool size 20, each query takes 10 ms, so each connection serves about 100 queries per second and 20 connections handle about 2,000 qps; extra requests queue in the pool instead of overwhelming the DB
Benefits: no per-request handshake cost; a hard cap on DB load; lower latency and steadier memory use

Things to consider: more connections is not faster, since cores x 2 plus disks is a good start; instances x pool size must stay below max_connections; PgBouncer transaction mode breaks session state such as prepared statements and SET; leaked connections drain the pool
Interview takeaway: size the pool small, calculate instances x pool size against the DB limit, and always return connections in a finally block

chapters.title: Partitioning
points: What it is: splitting one large table into smaller physical pieces (partitions) inside the same database server, by range, list or hash of a column
Why it exists: huge tables make scans, index maintenance, vacuum and deletes slow; smaller pieces are cheaper to scan, back up and drop
Used for: time-series and log tables, retention policies (drop a month), and queries that always filter on the partition key

How it works: CREATE TABLE events (id bigint, created_at date, payload jsonb) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at); one partition per month. SELECT ... WHERE created_at = '2026-03-05' reads only events_2026_03 (partition pruning); DROP TABLE events_2025_01 removes an old month instantly
Benefits: partition pruning cuts scanned data; instant bulk deletion by dropping a partition; smaller indexes per partition that fit in memory

Things to consider: queries without the partition key scan every partition; a poor key creates hot partitions (all today's data in one); partitions must be created ahead of time; it does not add machines, so that is sharding's job
Interview takeaway: partitioning splits data within one node to improve performance and manageability, while sharding splits it across nodes to scale out; choose the key from your query pattern

chapters.title: Replication
points: What it is: keeping copies of the same data on multiple servers, typically one primary that accepts writes and replicas that apply its changes
Why it exists: to survive a node failure (high availability), to serve more read traffic, and to place data near users
Used for: read replicas for analytics and read-heavy APIs, failover to a standby, and cross-region disaster recovery

How it works: the primary writes each change to its WAL and streams it to replicas. A user posts a comment (written to primary) and reloads, but the read goes to a replica 200 ms behind, so the comment is missing; fix by reading your own writes from the primary for a few seconds
Benefits: high availability through failover; read throughput scales with replica count; data closer to users; synchronous mode means no data loss, asynchronous mode keeps writes fast

Things to consider: replication lag gives stale reads; async failover can lose the last few commits; failover needs leader election and risks split-brain; replication scales reads, not writes; multi-leader setups need conflict resolution
Interview takeaway: replication gives availability and read scale, not write scale; state the sync-versus-async trade-off and handle read-your-writes explicitly

chapters.title: Sharding
points: What it is: horizontally splitting data across multiple independent database servers (shards), each holding a subset of rows chosen by a shard key
Why it exists: one machine eventually runs out of disk, memory or write throughput, and replication cannot fix write limits
Used for: very large user, order or message datasets, such as 1 billion users at 2 KB each (2 TB) across 8 shards

How it works: shard = hash(user_id) % 4. user_id 1001 maps to shard 1 and 1002 to shard 2, so each lookup by user_id hits exactly one server. Consistent hashing or a lookup directory lets you add shards without remapping every key
Benefits: near-linear scaling of storage and write throughput; smaller indexes per shard; failures limited to a subset of users

Things to consider: cross-shard joins and transactions are expensive or impossible; a skewed key creates a hot shard (a celebrity user); resharding is painful with plain modulo hashing; you also need a routing layer
Interview takeaway: shard last, after indexing, caching, replicas and partitioning; choose a high-cardinality key that matches your dominant access pattern and use consistent hashing

chapters.title: Database Concepts Cheatsheet
points: Indexing: B-tree turns O(n) scans into O(log n) lookups; leftmost prefix rule; cost is slower writes
Transactions and ACID: atomicity via undo, consistency via constraints, isolation via MVCC or locks, durability via WAL
Isolation levels: Read Committed stops dirty reads; Repeatable Read stops non-repeatable reads; Serializable stops phantoms and write skew
MVCC and locking: MVCC lets readers and writers coexist; locks (FOR UPDATE, or optimistic version checks) settle write-write conflicts; avoid deadlocks with a fixed lock order
Connection pooling: small pool, instances x pool size below max_connections, always release connections
Scaling order: index, then pool, then replicas for read scale, then partitioning, then sharding for write scale
